paper_title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Residual connections support optimization and information propagation in modern language models (He et al., 2016a,b; Vaswani et al., 2017; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b), and recent work improves language modeling and depth utilization by enriching this pathway (Pagliardini et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026). Hyper-Connections (HC) (Zhu et al., 2025) introduce (a) Training overhead (b) Saved activation storage (c) Downstream performance Figure 1 SimpleHC reduces training overhead while retaining competitive performance. (a) Additional training overhead relative to baseline with efficient implementations. (b) Storage retained for backward at sublayer boundaries (Section 5.5). (c) Average scores on 30B MoE models  (Table 4)  . multiple residual streams with learned read, write, and mixing operations for flexible information routing. The manifold-constrained variant, mHC (Xie et al., 2025), constrains residual mixing to improve training stability at scale. HC-based architectures, particularly mHC, have been adopted in frontier language models (Xu et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). Despite the growing adoption, these architectures remain insufficiently understood and costly to train: their gating and mixing operations introduce architectural complexity and non-negligible execution overhead, even under efficient implementations (Xie et al., 2025). key source of this overhead is repeated access to the expanded residual state: at every sublayer, HC-style mappings read and write streams of width to generate gates, aggregate inputs, and propagate updates. This memory traffic incurs costs not captured by FLOPs alone. In our end-to-end experiments with an efficient implementation, mHC adds 7% 27% training time over vanilla baseline (Figure 3(a)), despite adding less than 1% FLOPs. This motivates reconsidering the underlying read, write, and mixing interactions. We ask: Can simpler Hyper-Connections design reduce execution cost while preserving model quality and training stability at scale? In this work, we systematically study the Hyper-Connections architecture through three components: read gates, write gates, and residual mixing. We find that unconstrained mixing improves quality, but Sinkhorn constraints substantially reduce its benefit. Learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates each achieve quality comparable to mHC, with further gains from combining them. Our analysis also highlights the propagation risks of unconstrained mixing, leading us to select learned read/write gating with identity transitions as minimal effective structure that retains competitive quality while avoiding these risks. Without residual mixing, the additive structure lets scalar corrections exactly recover preceding output contributions for given gates, without materializing intermediate nC-dimensional states. Gate generation, however, still accesses the updated state at every sublayer. We reduce these accesses by computing layerspecific gates from common group-entry state, consolidating reads and deferring writes across sublayers. We call this execution scheme shared memory access. Together, these findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture through learned read/write gates without mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access. We also develop specialized kernels to translate this simplicity into training efficiency. As shown in Figure 1(a), SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% additional training cost at the largest tested scale and halves memory traffic from 18C to 9C per sublayer relative to fused mHC. It achieves downstream performance comparable to mHC and identityHC on 15B and 30B MoE models (Figure 1(c)). Analyses in Section 6 further support the design of SimpleHC. It also exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during training and remains stable under stress-test settings.

sections.content: We propose SimpleHC, Hyper-Connections architecture with simplified residual structure and execution scheme (Figure 2). It retains multiple residual streams and learned read/write gates while removing residual mixing. Shared memory access reduces repeated state access by generating layer-specific gates from group-entry states, batching reads, and deferring writes.

sections.title: 5.2 Understanding the Hyper-Connections Architecture
sections.content: We examine the roles and interactions of read/write gates and residual mixing in the HC architecture  (Table 2)  . HC and mHC share these components but differ in gate conditioning, parameterization, and mixing constraints. Except for HC variants, gates follow the parameterization in Section 3.1. Configurations. HC w/o mixing retains the HC parameterization but sets res = I; identityHC makes the same replacement in mHC. mHC w/o Sinkhorn and the unconstrained fixed-gate control use res = + reshape(ℓres), without exponentiation or Sinkhorn normalization. Restricted read/write replaces only the indicated gates input with the corresponding stream, using per-stream RMS normalization and 1 projection shared across streams; the other gate retains joint-state conditioning. Fixed read/write sets the indicated gate to 1/n or 1, respectively, while retaining the other components specified in the table. We observe: (i) Unconstrained mixing is effective, but Sinkhorn diminishes its gains. Retaining unconstrained mixing improves the average score in HC (rows 3 vs. 2). Under the mHC parameterization, unconstrained mixing achieves 56.2, versus 55.0 with Sinkhorn constraints and 55.4 with identity transitions (rows 46). Sinkhorn limits the benefit of mixing, leaving performance close to identityHC. (ii) Three components form two effective groups: read/write gating and unconstrained mixing. Without mixing, jointly learned read/write gates achieve an average score of 55.4; fixing either gate lowers it significantly, supporting their treatment as one group. Unconstrained mixing forms the other: with both gates fixed, it achieves 56.0 (row 12). Either group alone is comparable to mHC; combining them improves the score (row 4). (iii) Full-state conditioning improves model quality. With full-state inputs, loss is 1.660. Restricting read/write gates to stream-local inputs raises loss by 0.001/0.003 (rows 68), suggesting slightly greater sensitivity in write gates. Section 6.1 analyzes these findings and their implications for SimpleHC.

sections.title: 5.4 Evaluating SimpleHC at Larger Scale
sections.content: On the larger 30B-A2B model, SimpleHC matches mHC performance while simplifying both the residual structure and execution. As shown in Table 4, it achieves the same loss of 1.561 as mHC and identityHC and an average benchmark score of 63.1 versus 62.9 for mHC and 62.8 for identityHC. It achieves higher scores on MMLU, MATH, and C3, although it trails mHC on GSM8K and both methods on HumanEval. These results support the scalability of SimpleHC.

sections.title: 5.5 Translating Simplicity into Training Efficiency
sections.content: We compare end-to-end training overhead against the baseline across scales from = 1024 to = 6144 (matching frontier models (Xu et al., 2026; Tencent Hy Team, 2026)). Details are provided in Appendix A.2. With the efficient implementations, SimpleHC achieves the lowest overhead across all tested scales (Figure 3(a)). At the smallest scale, overhead is 6.3%, versus 26.8% for mHC and 10.1% for identityHC. Despite matching forward activation traffic, mHC incurs additional mixing and Sinkhorn costs, explaining its larger gap from identityHC at smaller scales. Relative overhead generally decreases with width: HC operations scale linearly at fixed n, whereas expert projections scale quadratically when expert width grows proportionally. At the largest tested scale, SimpleHC cuts overhead from approximately 7.0% for both baselines to 2.4%, eliminating about two-thirds. We additionally compare against xHC, promising approach to scaling residual-stream capacity (Zhang et al., 2026). At = 6144, its training overhead is 27.7%, compared with approximately 7.0% for mHC and 2.4% for SimpleHC (Figure 4). These results position SimpleHC as one of the most efficient HC variants evaluated for scaling foundation models. Specialized kernels require substantial engineering effort, limiting wider adoption. sections.title: 6 Analysis
sections.content: We analyze the design and training stability of SimpleHC. Three conclusions emerge: (i) learned read/write gating provides minimal effective residual structure; (ii) gating decisions vary across sublayers yet remain predictable from shared group-entry state; (iii) SimpleHC remains stable under stress and exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training. 9 Figure 4 Training overhead compared with mHC and xHC. All methods use efficient implementations, with overhead measured relative to the vanilla residual baseline. xHC uses 16 residual streams with 4 active streams; mHC and SimpleHC use 4 residual streams.

sections.title: 6.1 A Minimal Structure for Hyper-Connections
sections.content: To combine architectural simplicity, competitive performance, and robust scaling, we select learned read/write gating without mixing as minimal effective residual structure for Hyper-Connections. This avoids the propagation risks of cumulative residual mixing, as analyzed below. Learned read/write gating and unconstrained mixing form two effective groups: each achieves performance comparable to mHC, with further gains when combined  (Table 2)  . Appendix compares their weighting mechanisms. However, unconstrained mixing repeatedly transforms earlier contributions through residual matrix products, risking cumulative amplification and training instability (Xie et al., 2025). We observe unconstrained mixing with fixed gates produces larger peak residual-path coefficients than identityHC, consistent with these amplification risks (Figure 7, Appendix D.1). Sinkhorn constraints mitigate these risks (Xie et al., 2025), but constrained mixing adds little benefit over learned read/write gating alone. We therefore retain learned gates without mixing and use full-state inputs for better loss and benchmark scores  (Table 2)  . Full-state and stream-local conditioning incur the same residual-state input traffic, as both read all streams.

sections.title: 6.2 Why Shared Memory Access Is Effective
sections.content: We examine why shared memory access benefits from layer-specific gates and remains effective with shared inputs through gate variation and predictability analyses. Gate variation across sublayers. Read and write gates exhibit distinct allocation patterns across sublayers of the 15B identityHC model (Figures 8(a) and 5(a)). These differences motivate retaining layer-specific gates under shared inputs, consistent with their advantage over gate reuse  (Table 3)  . Predictability from the group-entry state. We examine whether subsequent gates are predictable from the group-entry state to assess the feasibility of sharing gate inputs. We train layer-specific predictors to recover subsequent read/write gates of frozen 15B identityHC model from the group-entry state. The predictors use the SimpleHC parameterization and are initialized from the corresponding teacher gate parameters. Only predictors are trained. The Frozen teacher gates baseline uses these mappings without training. In Figure 5(b), it predicts write gates more accurately than uniform random gates (MAE 0.0504 vs. 0.4086), indicating predictive ability from earlier inputs even without adaptation. Training further reduces MAE to 0.0103, suggesting that layer-specific mappings closely approximate subsequent gates from shared inputs and supporting the shared memory access design. Read gates show the same trend (Figure 8(b)). sections.title: 6.3 Does Simplification Compromise Training Stability?
sections.content: Training stability is essential for reliable scaling, as instabilities absent in smaller models can emerge at larger scales (Wortsman et al., 2024). We examine whether the simplifications in SimpleHC compromise training stability. During 15B training, SimpleHC shows smaller gradient-norm fluctuations and lower rolling standard deviation than mHC and identityHC early after warmup (Figure 6(a)); all three reach comparable ranges later. Shared-input gating may reduce sensitivity to within-group state fluctuations by conditioning decisions on an earlier state, loosely analogous to stabilization through historical averaging. This could contribute to smoother training of SimpleHC. To emulate large-scale training stability challenges, we stress-test 230B-A6B MoE models at 10 the reference learning rate. In Figure 6(b), mHC exhibits gradient spikes reaching approximately 1.9 106, while SimpleHC and identityHC maintain bounded gradient norms. Appendix details the settings and analyzes potential causes of mHC instability.

sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: Hyper-Connections and Variants. Hyper-Connections expand the residual pathway into multiple streams with learned read, write, and mixing operations (Zhu et al., 2025). Subsequent work constrains mixing to doubly stochastic matrices (Xie et al., 2025), reduces constraint-enforcement costs (Yang and Gao, 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Dandachi and Diggs-Galligan, 2026), or explores other constraints for stable propagation and stream diversity (Liu et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026). Other designs modify read/write structures (Qiu et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026) or use sparse updates to support more streams (Zhang et al., 2026). Understanding and Simplifying Hyper-Connections. Recent analyses reveal uneven stream utilization, redundancy, and concentrated read/write routing in HC models (Peng et al., 2026; Alimaskina et al., 2026). Prior work also reports that removing residual mixing can largely preserve model quality (Guo et al., 2026), with related evidence from finetuning (Oldenburg et al., 2026). These observations motivate examining which interactions account for the benefits. Our study identifies learned read/write gating and unconstrained mixing as two independently effective groups, while showing that Sinkhorn constraints diminish the gains from mixing. These findings explain why learned gating alone remains competitive with mHC (Xie et al., 2025) and motivate an additive structure whose execution we further simplify through shared memory access. Efficient Execution of Residual Aggregation. Richer residual pathways introduce storage and datamovement costs beyond their arithmetic overhead. Prior work reduces these costs through block-wise aggregation and staged computation (Team et al., 2026), kernel fusion and recomputation (Xie et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026), and optimized multi-stream execution (Zhang et al., 2026). SimpleHC further reduces repeated residual-state access across sublayers by sharing gate inputs while retaining layer-specific parameters. Together with the additive residual structure, this permits consolidated reads and deferred writes, with scalar corrections preserving sequential output contributions for the chosen gates.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we study how the components of the Hyper-Connections architecture contribute to model performance and training cost. Our study identifies learned read/write gating as minimal effective structure, while unconstrained mixing offers gains with propagation risks. Beyond removing mixing, we introduce shared memory access to reduce repeated residual-state accesses, with gate analyses supporting layer-specific mappings conditioned on shared inputs. Together, they form SimpleHC, simplifying residual structure and execution. SimpleHC matches mHC performance on 15B and 30B MoE models, reduces additional training overhead from 7.0% to 2.4% at the largest tested scale, and exhibits smoother gradient dynamics while remaining stable under stress. SimpleHC thus combines architectural simplicity, execution efficiency, training stability, and scalability.

sections.content: This section details the measurements and experimental protocols for the analyses in Sections 6.1 and 6.2. sections.title: E Training Stability Details
sections.content: This section details the stress-test design, training dynamics, and instability diagnostics supporting Section 6.3. E.1 Stress-Test Design and Settings To emulate stability challenges in large-scale training, we combine 64 layers, 512 routed experts with top-8 routing, and learning rate 10 the reference value. This stresses optimization through longer propagation path, higher sparsity, and larger updates. hidden width of 2816 keeps activated parameters near 6B, yielding 230B-A6B model. The experiment tests robustness under these combined pressures rather than isolating individual factors. 21 Figure 9 Training loss under stress. All runs cover the same 28,000 steps. We show per-step losses and their 100-step moving averages. The inset enlarges the low-loss region over steps 2,00028,000. (a) Attention output (b) FFN output Figure 10 Attention and FFN output standard deviations under stress. Lines show 100-step moving averages; shaded bands show the minimum and maximum within each window. Both panels use logarithmic vertical axes and cover the same 28,000 steps. All variants use the backbone in Table 8. MLA alternates full and sliding-window attention in 1:3 pattern, with 72 heads and window size 512. The first FFN is dense with width 7936; the remaining 63 use experts of width 832 and one shared expert. Training uses BF16, microbatch size 1, and Muon with momentum 0.95, weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The WSD schedule uses 4,000 linear warmup steps, followed by the peak learning rate throughout the comparison window. HC variants use = 4; mHC uses 20 Sinkhorn iterations, and SimpleHC uses = 4. E.2 Training Dynamics Standard training. During 15B training, SimpleHC shows smaller gradient-norm fluctuations early after warmup than mHC and identityHC, with comparable ranges later (Figure 6(a)). The maximum 1,000-step rolling standard deviation after warmup is 0.032 for SimpleHC, versus 0.206 for mHC and 0.248 for identityHC, indicating smoother standard training. Stress testing. Under stress, mHC exhibits gradient spikes reaching approximately 1.9 106, whereas SimpleHC and identityHC remain bounded (Figure 6(b)). These spikes in mHC are accompanied by loss spikes (Figure 9) and growing branch-output scales, especially in the FFN. SimpleHC and identityHC show no comparable sustained growth (Figure 10), supporting stable training despite the structural and execution simplifications. 22 E.3 Analysis of Stress-Test Results SimpleHC and identityHC maintain stable optimization under the combined stress setting, indicating that removing residual mixing, with or without shared gate inputs, can preserve training stability. SimpleHC remains comparable to identityHC despite sharing gate inputs across sublayers. In contrast, mHC exhibits instability in both forward activations and backward gradients. To investigate this behavior, we inspect its branch outputs, residual mixing matrices, and gradient paths. In captured early-layer MoE event, an input RMS of 0.294 produced branch-output RMS of 2.31 104 before write gating, locating the initial large values in the FFN rather than residual mixing at this sublayer. In the observed stress setting, 20 Sinkhorn iterations did not always suffice to produce doubly stochastic matrix. In one captured case, row sums remained (2, 1, 0.5, 0.5), increasing same-token RMS from 5.42 104 to 7.50 104. Mixing could therefore further amplify existing FFN outliers. These observations also suggest possible rationale for the SwiGLU clamping used in DeepSeek-V4 (Xu et al., 2026): limiting FFN outliers before they enter the residual pathway. Residual mixing also introduces an additional gradient path because res depends on the input. For = res(X)X, the differential is dY = resdX + (dH res)X: the first term propagates through the fixed matrix, while the second captures changes in the mixing matrix itself. In one captured backward spike, the gate-input gradient norm was approximately 9.4 that of the fixed-matrix path in the same call. Bounds computed from the recorded read/write gates and upstream gradients made their contributions negligible, implicating the dynamic mixing path. Whether this anomaly reflects mathematical sensitivity or numerical effects in backward remains unresolved. Identity transitions set dH res = 0, eliminating this additional path, consistent with the stable training observed in identityHC and SimpleHC.
